cells.tense: You are here in this, taking in what people carry and saying what is fair.
cells.ask: Choose one thing you've been leaving open and settle it today, on what you already have.
cells.core:
You can feel what's happening and still say what's fair about it. Not the one keeping score on the side — you take in what people are carrying, including what they'd rather you missed, and you call it straight. That lands, and it's landing now.

The ground under it is a road you only ever see one step down. You don't know how the whole thing turns out, and you decide anyway, which is the only way anything gets decided. To keep this, let the next step show up without demanding the one after it — that costs something. Wait for the full picture and the call you'd make fairly today is the one you'll make unfairly later.

cells.tense: You are living past this moment, braced for a fairness that has not arrived yet.
cells.ask: Name one outcome you are trying to force, then leave it alone for a day and watch what happens.
cells.core:
You're running the fairness check ahead of the situation that needs it. Before anyone has said anything, you've worked out who should get what, how it should go, what would make it right — an answer to a question nobody asked yet. The judging has gotten out ahead of the thing being judged.

What you're after is a plain sense of what's right without all the calculation, give and take that just moves. Pushing for it early is what keeps it away, because nobody can meet a verdict that arrived before they did. Holding something steady doesn't mean gripping it. Stay with the moment as it is and let the fair answer come once there's something in front of you to answer.

cells.tense: You are at a door that closed behind you, not quite in the room.
cells.ask: Describe one thing you noticed today, exactly, before you decide what it means.
cells.core:
The judging part is quiet right now, and it's been quiet a while. Calling something fair or unfair lost its footing along the way, so you stopped calling it, and the not-calling settled in. So things happen around you and you watch from a small distance, keeping your read to yourself even when it's accurate.

What's starved isn't feeling — that's all still there. It's the part that can look at something honestly and say what it saw. You don't get that back by making yourself feel more. You get it back by being accurate about small things: one square inch of what's in front of you, described right. That's the muscle that pulls the other one back.

cells.tense: You are already making the call and describing it as though it made itself.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to someone or to the room, that one recent thing you called fair was your call.
cells.core:
You tell it like the situation decided itself. The facts were what they were, the reasonable thing was clear, anybody would have landed where you landed — but you're the one who looked at how people were feeling and said what should happen. That judgment keeps running. You just don't sign it.

The pen has been passed to the circumstances, and calling it your call got filed as arrogant or risky somewhere. Underneath is the simpler thing you already do well: you can look at something without forcing a verdict, and your read lands clean when you don't argue for it. Signing one call won't make it heavier. It puts the pen back in your hand.

A reader could reasonably say they've never felt balanced about any of this, only careful, so the ask in each cell has to be worth doing on its own even if my read is wrong about them. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line about how rare or hard-won their fairness is — it flatters the map, so it's gone; the sheet lines are short claims they could push back on and still use.
